docs.title: iteraSim Eddy — User Guide
docs.text:
Navigating Possibilities in Fluid Dynamics

iteraSim Eddy is a desktop application that drives OpenFOAM end to end — case setup, meshing, solver runs and post-processing — with an AI copilot across the whole workflow rather than bolted onto one step.

This guide takes a new user from a blank machine to a finished, verified simulation. Everything here is the real application, screen by screen.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• 1 Installation

    Requirements, the AppImage, and automatic OpenFOAM detection. One file, no root, no dependencies.

  • 2 First launch & account

    Create an account, sign in on a second machine, and what Free gives you versus Pro.

  • 3 Tour of the interface

    The three panes, the tool rail, Case Builder, Solver Workshop, the Copilot and the mesh preview.

  • 4 Common workflows

    Open a case, generate a mesh, run the solver — plus a full worked lid-driven-cavity example, screen by screen.

docs.title: The worked example
docs.text:
If you only read one section, make it 4.6 Worked example — lid-driven cavity at Re = 1000.

It is the standard CFD verification problem, it has a published answer, and it tells you whether a surprising result is your setup or the solver. A correct run reproduces Ghia, Ghia & Shin (1982) along the vertical centreline to well under one percent, with the primary vortex centred near (0.53, 0.56).

Why start with a benchmark

Running a case with a known answer first means every later surprise is information about your problem, not about your installation.

docs.text:

docs.title: 4 Common workflows
docs.text: The five things you'll actually do 90% of the time.

docs.title: 4.1 Open or create a case
docs.text:
Two ways to start:

  • Open existing: File → Open Workspace → point at any OpenFOAM case directory (must contain system/, constant/, and a 0/ folder).
  • Create new: click New Case in the left sidebar to open the Case Builder wizard — pick a solver, mesh source, and boundary types.

docs.title: 4.2 Chat with the copilot
docs.text:
The Copilot panel on the right of the screen is where you talk to the AI. Ask questions like:

  • "Why is my kOmegaSST diverging after 200 iterations?"
  • "Set up a Boussinesq-buoyant simulation for this geometry."
  • "Fix the boundary conditions so the outlet doesn't back-flow."

The copilot has full visibility of your case files — it reads controlDict, fvSchemes, the boundary field files, and the mesh statistics before answering. When it suggests a change, you'll see a Preview change button — nothing is written to disk until you approve it.

Tip

The status bar shows how many tokens you've used this month. Free-tier users see the counter turn amber near 40k tokens and red at 50k.

docs.title: 4.3 Generate a mesh
docs.text:
The Mesh tab in the left sidebar offers three routes:

  • blockMesh — for simple rectangular / cylindrical domains, driven by the visual wizard.
  • snappyHexMesh — for STL-based geometries, with layer and refinement controls.
  • Gmsh — import a .msh file; Eddy runs gmshToFoam automatically.

After meshing, the mesh preview loads in the centre viewport. Rotate with left-click, pan with right-click, zoom with the scroll wheel.

Note

The in-app preview is a sanity check — for full post-processing hand the case off to ParaView with the toolbar button, which opens ParaView with the mesh loaded.

docs.title: 4.4 Run the solver
docs.text:
Click Run in the top toolbar. Eddy launches the solver in an embedded terminal at the bottom of the screen, and the Residuals panel starts plotting the log in real time. You can:

  • Pause / resume / stop the run from the toolbar.
  • Edit controlDict mid-run — Eddy detects runTimeModifiable true and reloads parameters at the next iteration.
  • Watch the health indicator (Converging / Stagnated / Diverging) update live.

docs.title: 4.5 Send results to a cluster
docs.text:
The Cluster tab in the left sidebar sets up an SSH profile for your HPC. Once configured you can:

  • Upload the current case to the cluster with one click.
  • Submit a Slurm / LSF job from a template — Eddy fills in the case path and MPI process count.
  • Watch the remote solver output stream back to the local console.
  • Rsync results back for post-processing in ParaView.

docs.title: 4.6 Worked example — lid-driven cavity at Re = 1000
docs.text:
A short case with a published answer, so you can tell whether a surprising result is your setup or the solver. The lid-driven cavity is the standard CFD verification problem: a square box whose top wall slides sideways.

Reynolds number is set by Re = U·L/ν. With a 1 m box and a lid at 1 m/s, ν = 1e-3 gives Re = 1000. In the Case Builder:

  • Solver — icoFoam.
  • Mesh — dimensions 1 × 1 × 0.1, cells 128 × 128 × 1.
  • Patches — movingWall on top (wall); fixedWalls on left, right, bottom (wall); frontAndBack on front, back (empty).
  • Boundary condition — override U on movingWall to fixedValue, uniform (1 0 0).
  • Physics — nu = 1e-3, laminar.
  • Runtime — endTime 40, deltaT 0.002, writeInterval 5.

Note

The single cell in the third direction, with both its faces set to empty, is what makes the case 2D. Miss it and OpenFOAM happily solves a one-cell-thick 3D problem instead.

Run it, then compare the horizontal velocity along the vertical centreline against Ghia, Ghia & Shin (1982), the benchmark every CFD code is checked against. A correct run reproduces it to well under one percent, with the primary vortex centred near (0.53, 0.56). If your numbers are close, your installation and your workflow are both sound.

Tip

Re is set by viscosity here, not by lid speed. To move to Re = 100 leave the lid at 1 m/s and raise nu to 1e-2 — handy when you want a quicker, steadier case to practise on.

docs.title: 4.7 The same case, screen by screen
docs.text:
Every screen below is the real application running the lid-driven cavity from 4.6, in order, from a cold start to a finished solve.

The three panes. Tool rail on the far left, the workspace in the middle, and the Copilot on the right. The terminal sits along the bottom and the status bar reports OpenFOAM version, core count and solver state. Case Builder, opened from the second icon in the rail. The seven steps run down the left; Live Summary on the right updates as you fill them in, so you can see the case taking shape before anything is written. Step 1 — Case. Name the case, choose the solver, and set the parent directory. The line beneath shows exactly where the case will be written. Below that sit the built-in templates. Choosing the Lid-driven cavity template fills every step at once: Live Summary flips to icoFoam, 3 patches, laminar, and the field list narrows to U and p. Nothing is on disk yet. Step 2 — Mesh. A 0.1 m square, 20 × 20 × 1 cells. Note the line under the cell counts: 400 cells · 2D (set front/back patches to empty), which is the rule that makes this a 2D case rather than a one-cell-thick 3D one. Step 3 — Boundaries. movingWall takes the top face, fixedWalls the other three, and frontAndBack is typed empty — the 2D treatment from the previous step, made concrete. Step 6 — Run. endTime, deltaT and writeInterval go straight into controlDict. For a transient solver such as icoFoam the interval is a time, not an iteration count. Step 7 — Review. The exact file list and the target path, before committing. All seven steps show green. After Generate Case: eight files written and the case loaded into the workspace. The Copilot picks it up immediately — note the new Run cavity button in the chat panel. The Solve tab. Solver configuration and parallel settings on the left, a live 3D preview of the meshed domain in the middle, and mesh-quality readouts on the right with a one-click checkMesh. A finished run. The terminal carries the usual OpenFOAM output — GAMG pressure solves, continuity errors, ExecutionTime — and the Copilot confirms icoFoam finished (exit=0) with the case path and a pointer to the Post-Process tab.

Results land in the case directory as time folders — 0.1, 0.2 … 0.5 for this case — each holding U, p and phi. Post-processing happens in ParaView, which the toolbar button launches.

ParaView opens as an empty session — the case is not handed to it automatically — so load it yourself. It takes four steps:

  • File → Open, then pick the .foam file in your case directory. If there is not one, create it with touch cavity.foam: an empty file with that extension is what ParaView reads.
  • Press Apply in the Properties panel. Nothing appears until you do.
  • Add a Cell Data to Point Data filter. OpenFOAM stores results per cell; this interpolates them to the mesh points so the field is smooth rather than blocky.
  • In the colouring dropdown choose U and Magnitude, then drag the time slider to the last step.
The cavity in ParaView at t = 0.5 s. The pipeline on the left runs cavity.foam → CellDatatoPointData1; the toolbar shows the field (U), the component (Magnitude) and the representation (Surface). The colour bar is labelled in m/s. The same field on its own. The lid drags fluid along the top at 1 m/s and the momentum diffuses downward, leaving the lower half nearly still — the expected result at this Reynolds number, and your confirmation that the whole chain works.

Note

From here the usual ParaView tools apply: Stream Tracer to show the recirculation, Plot Over Line down the vertical centreline to compare against benchmark data, and the camera controls to zoom into the corner vortices.

docs.title: 4.8 Not in this release
docs.text:
Two panels you may have seen in earlier previews are disabled in v1.0.0:

  • Dataset Generator — parameter-study batch runner for building ML training sets.
  • ML Training — in-app FNO / PINN / CNO training on OpenFOAM datasets.

Both are still under active development and will return in a future release. If you were relying on them, drop us a line at info@iterasim.in — early-access users get the beta build first.

docs.title: 2 First launch & account
docs.text: Register once, sign in on every machine you install Eddy on.

docs.title: 2.1 Create an account
docs.text:
Click the account icon in the top-right corner. A sign-in dialog opens with two tabs: Login and Register.

  • Pick Register.
  • Enter your work email and a password of at least 8 characters.
  • Click Create account.

Your account is created immediately on the Free plan with 50,000 AI tokens for the current month. You are logged in automatically — the top-right badge now shows your email and plan.

docs.title: 2.2 Signing in on another machine
docs.text:
Use the same email and password on any other Eddy install. Your plan and monthly token bucket follow the account, not the machine.

Tip

Forgot your password? Email info@iterasim.in — self-serve reset is on the roadmap.

docs.title: 2.3 Free vs Pro at a glance
docs.text: Free Pro Price €0 $29 / month Monthly AI tokens 50,000 5,000,000 OpenFOAM copilot Yes (your own API key) Yes (managed keys) Curated RAG knowledge – Yes Priority model routing – Yes (Gemini 2.5 / Claude) ParaView / cluster Yes Yes Email support Best-effort 1 business day

docs.title: 7 Frequently asked questions
docs.text: Answers to the questions we get most often. If yours isn't here, section 8 tells you where to ask.

docs.title: Is my case data ever sent to iteraSim's servers?
docs.text: No. Case files — meshes, dict files, solver results — stay on your machine. When you chat with Copilot, only the specific file snippets Copilot needs to answer are sent to the AI model provider (Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, or your local Ollama, depending on your setting). We never store your files, and the model providers we route through are configured to not train on your prompts.

docs.title: Does Eddy need an internet connection?
docs.text: Only for the AI copilot and, if you use them, cloud sync + cluster upload. The full local workflow — Case Builder, blockMesh / snappyHexMesh / Gmsh, running the solver, ParaView handoff — works entirely offline. If you point Copilot at a local Ollama model (AI Extensions panel), even the AI runs offline.

docs.title: Do I need OpenFOAM installed separately?
docs.text: Yes. Eddy is the interface; OpenFOAM is the engine. Install any recent version (v2312 or newer). Ubuntu / Debian: sudo apt install openfoam2312-default. Fedora: sudo dnf install openfoam. Eddy auto-detects it at startup — the version shows in the bottom-right status bar.

docs.title: Which OpenFOAM versions are supported?
docs.text: OpenFOAM v2306 and later (the ESI-OpenCFD fork) are fully supported. The OpenFOAM Foundation fork (v9, v10, v11) works for most cases but some solvers have slightly different names — Copilot handles the translation transparently. foam-extend is not officially supported.

docs.title: What is the "backend", and why does the status bar say Offline?
docs.text:
Eddy runs a small Python service on your own machine at 127.0.0.1:8000. It drives the solver pipeline and, on Pro, serves your managed model access. It starts automatically with the app and is local-only — it never listens on an external interface and your case files never leave the machine.

The status bar tells you which mode you're in: ● Ready / LIVE means the backend is up; ○ Offline / LOCAL means it isn't. If it's Offline, press ⟳ Start Backend. See section 6 for the full walkthrough — in particular, a Pro user seeing "No API key configured" is seeing a backend problem, not a key problem.

Simulation work is unaffected either way: meshing, solving and post-processing are all local and run with the backend down.

docs.title: Can I use Eddy without a paid account?
docs.text: Yes — the Free tier includes 50,000 AI tokens per month and the entire local workflow. Bring your own Google Gemini / Anthropic / OpenAI key in AI Extensions, or point at a local Ollama model, and you have no monthly limit at all — iteraSim doesn't charge to run Eddy itself, only for our managed AI routing on Pro.

docs.title: What's a "token" and how many does a typical question use?
docs.text: Roughly, 1 token ≈ 0.75 English words. A short question and answer with Copilot typically uses 500–2,000 tokens. A long debugging session where Copilot reads 5–10 case files might use 20,000–40,000. The 50k monthly Free budget covers ~10 typical sessions, or ~100 short questions.

docs.title: Copilot changed a file and now my case won't run. How do I undo?
docs.text: Every Copilot-driven change is recorded in per-case history. Open the file that changed, right-click in the editor → Revert to previous version. Or use the top-level File → Case history to see and undo everything from the last N sessions.

docs.title: Can I run cases in parallel on my laptop (multiple cores)?
docs.text: Yes. When you launch a solver from the Case Builder or Wizard, tick Run in parallel and pick a core count. Eddy runs decomposePar automatically with the scotch method, launches with mpirun, and reconstructs the result at the end. Everything is transparent — the case looks single-processor from your perspective.

docs.title: How do I import geometry from SolidWorks / Fusion 360 / CATIA?
docs.text: Export as STEP (preferred) or STL from your CAD tool. In Eddy, drag the file into the Project Navigator or use Case Builder → Geometry → Import. STL is meshed directly by snappyHexMesh; STEP is converted to STL first (Eddy does that in one click via Gmsh) and then meshed.

docs.title: Can I share a case with a colleague?
docs.text: Two ways: (1) zip up the case folder (Right-click in Navigator → Compress case — Eddy skips the huge processor*/ directories automatically) and email them the zip. (2) Use the Cloud Storage panel to sync to a shared bucket / Drive folder they also have access to. Both include the full case setup; only the solver results are optional.

docs.title: Does Eddy work on macOS or Windows?
docs.text: Linux is the primary platform (this AppImage). A Windows build ships separately as a .exe installer that runs the backend in WSL. macOS is not officially supported yet — it's on the roadmap, subscribe on our website to be notified.

docs.title: How do I upgrade Eddy itself when a new version ships?
docs.text: Download the new AppImage from your account page, replace the old file at ~/Applications/, and launch. Your settings, cases, and history all persist — they live outside the AppImage (see the appendix for paths). The self-installed menu entry auto-updates on first launch of the new build.

docs.title: Can I use Eddy for commercial / consulting work?
docs.text: Yes on all tiers. Pro and Team include commercial-use terms; Enterprise adds an indemnification clause. See https://iterasim.in/terms for the full text.

docs.title: 1 Installation
docs.text: Linux only in this guide. Windows users: see IteraSim_Windows_Build_Guide.pdf.

docs.title: 1.1 System requirements
docs.text:
• A 64-bit Linux distribution (Ubuntu 22.04+, Fedora 39+, Debian 12+, or equivalent).
  • glibc 2.35 or newer.
  • At least 4 GB RAM (8 GB recommended for meshing).
  • OpenFOAM v2312 or later installed (native or via apt install openfoam). Eddy detects it automatically at startup.
  • Internet connection for the AI copilot. The solver itself runs fully offline.

docs.title: 1.2 Download
docs.text:
Download the single-file installer from your account page or a link provided by iteraSim. The file is called:

iteraSim-Eddy-1.0.0.AppImage

This is a fully self-contained AppImage. No apt install, no root, no dependencies to unpack — the app runs on any modern Linux distribution straight out of the file.

docs.title: 1.3 Install and launch
docs.text:
Move the AppImage somewhere permanent first — a good choice is ~/Applications/. Then open a terminal in that folder and run:

mkdir -p ~/Applications
mv iteraSim-Eddy-1.0.0.AppImage ~/Applications/
chmod +x ~/Applications/iteraSim-Eddy-1.0.0.AppImage
~/Applications/iteraSim-Eddy-1.0.0.AppImage

That is the entire installation. The main window opens directly. There is no separate installer step — the AppImage is the app.

docs.title: Automatic system-menu integration
docs.text:
On its first launch, Eddy registers itself with your Linux desktop environment: it writes a .desktop entry into ~/.local/share/applications/ and copies the logo into ~/.local/share/icons/hicolor/. From that point on, iteraSim Eddy appears in your Activities / Applications menu with its icon — you can pin it to the dock and launch it like any other installed program. No terminal required after the first run.

Tip

If you move the AppImage to a different folder later, launch it once from the new location. Eddy detects the move and updates the menu entry automatically.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
Because nothing was installed system-wide, uninstalling is three deletions:

rm ~/Applications/iteraSim-Eddy-1.0.0.AppImage
rm ~/.local/share/applications/iterasim-eddy.desktop
rm ~/.local/share/icons/hicolor/512x512/apps/iterasim-eddy.png
# Optional: also remove your local settings + cases
rm -rf ~/.iterasim ~/.config/iteraSim

docs.title: 1.4 OpenFOAM detection
docs.text:
At first launch, Eddy scans your system for an OpenFOAM installation. If found, the version appears in the bottom-right status bar. If not, you'll see OpenFOAM: not found — install it and re-launch:

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install openfoam2312-default

# Fedora
sudo dnf install openfoam

# Arch
yay -S openfoam-org

docs.title: 8 Support & community
docs.text: Where to write when something breaks, and where to hang out with other Eddy users.

docs.title: 8.1 Report a bug or ask a question
docs.text:
Three channels, listed from best to fastest:

Channel Best for Response time Community forum Any question, bug, or feature idea — searchable so others benefit too. Community-driven; iteraSim replies within 1–2 days Email — info@iterasim.in Billing issues, account problems, anything you'd rather keep private. 1 business day on Free, 1 business day guaranteed on Pro Priority support (Team / Enterprise) Production incidents affecting your team's work. 4 business hours

docs.title: 8.2 Community forum
docs.text:
The Eddy community forum lives at:

https://github.com/iterasim/eddy-community/discussions

You need a free GitHub account to post. The forum is organised into:

  • General — Q&A: ask anything about using Eddy or OpenFOAM.
  • Bug reports: something isn't working the way the documentation says it should.
  • Feature requests: ideas for the next release. We read every one.
  • Show & tell: share cases you've solved with Eddy. Screenshots welcome.
  • Announcements: iteraSim posts new release notes here.

Tip

When reporting a bug, please include: your Linux distribution + version, OpenFOAM version (bottom-right status bar), Eddy version (Help → About), and the exact steps to reproduce. If Eddy crashed, attach the log file from ~/.config/iteraSim/logs/.

docs.title: 8.3 Stay up to date
docs.text:
• Release notes: https://iterasim.in/changelog
  • Blog & CFD tips: https://iterasim.in/blog
  • LinkedIn: linkedin.com/company/iterasim
  • Newsletter: monthly, opt in on your account page.

docs.title: 3 Tour of the interface
docs.text: Every icon in the sidebar, one paragraph each. Skim once, come back when you need it.

docs.title: 3.1 The three panes
docs.text:
The Eddy window is split into three columns you can drag to resize:

  • Left sidebar — icon rail (the tools listed below) plus a context panel that changes with the icon you pick.
  • Centre workspace — the file editor, mesh preview, or wizard content. Whatever you're actively working on lives here.
  • Right Copilot panel — the AI chat that has full visibility of your case files. Collapsible with the toolbar toggle.

Along the bottom is a status bar that shows: OpenFOAM version, current case path, token usage this month, and connection state to the AI backend. A red or amber counter next to your email means you're approaching the monthly token limit.

Tip

Hover any icon in the rail to see what that tool does before you click it. The panel you are in is highlighted, so you can always tell where you are.

docs.title: 3.2 Project Navigator
docs.text:
Icon: waves · Purpose: browse and open OpenFOAM cases, solver directories, mesh files, and results.

This is your starting point. Point it at any folder containing system/, constant/, and a 0/ directory and Eddy recognises it as a case. From the tree you can:

  • Double-click any file to open it in the editor (dict files, .foam files, logs, STLs).
  • Right-click a .foam file → Open in ParaView (Eddy launches it with the case pre-loaded).
  • Right-click an STL/STEP → Open in FreeCAD for geometry inspection.
  • Drag any folder into the sidebar to add it as a workspace shortcut.

Note

The Navigator watches the file system in real time. Edits made outside Eddy (by ParaView, an external editor, or a solver run) show up in the tree within a second.

docs.title: 3.3 Case Builder
docs.text:
Icon: dashboard grid + C badge · Purpose: build an OpenFOAM case form-by-form without editing dict files by hand.

Nine solvers have a full Case Builder template: simpleFoam, porousSimpleFoam, pimpleFoam, pisoFoam, icoFoam, buoyantSimpleFoam, buoyantPimpleFoam, rhoSimpleFoam and rhoPimpleFoam. The dropdown lists the wider OpenFOAM family too, but anything without a template is marked not yet supported — pick one of the nine, or build that case by hand in the Project Navigator. For a supported solver the builder walks you through every dictionary it needs:

  • Physics — kinematic viscosity, transport model, and turbulence model.
  • Boundary conditions — per-patch dropdowns matched to what the solver actually accepts (no more digging through the header of every BC file).
  • Numerics — a sane fvSchemes and fvSolution preset for the chosen solver, editable per-term.
  • Runtime — start/end time, writeInterval, adjustable time-step controls.

Set Case name and Parent directory before you write — the write button stays disabled until both are filled in, which is the usual reason it looks like nothing happens. Eddy then writes each dictionary in turn and shows a live counter; if a file fails it stops and tells you which one, leaving the rest in place so you can retry. The finished case is loaded into the Navigator automatically, ready to run.

Tip

You don't have to touch the forms yourself. Ask Copilot — e.g. "set up a Boussinesq buoyant case for this geometry with air at 300 K" — and it drives the Case Builder for you, previewing every change before writing.

docs.title: 3.4 Solver Workshop
docs.text:
Icon: code brackets + S badge · Purpose: clone, edit, and compile OpenFOAM's C++ solvers when a built-in solver doesn't quite fit.

Use cases: adding a custom source term, modifying a turbulence model, wiring in a new transport equation, or just reading the solver source to understand it. Workshop gives you:

  • One-click clone of any solver in your OpenFOAM install into ~/IteraSim/solvers/.
  • Syntax-highlighted C++ editor with jump-to-definition across the solver's files.
  • Compile button that runs wmake and streams the log to a panel below the editor — errors are clickable and jump to the line.
  • Copilot integration: highlight code and ask "turn this into a compressible variant" or "add a Coriolis source term".

Note

The Workshop is a power-user tool. If you've never touched OpenFOAM C++ before, start with the Case Builder — 95% of simulations don't need custom solvers.

docs.title: 3.5 CFD Workflow Wizard
docs.text:
Icon: compass + W badge · Purpose: a guided step-by-step flow for setting up a full simulation from scratch, in the right order.

Where the Case Builder is form-driven and non-linear (jump to whichever tab you want), the Wizard is a linear pipeline that mirrors the real CFD workflow:

  • 1 Geometry — import STL/STEP, run checkMesh, or generate primitives.
  • 2 Mesh — pick blockMesh / snappyHexMesh / Gmsh and configure.
  • 3 Physics — pick solver and boundary conditions.
  • 4 Solve — run and monitor residuals.
  • 5 Post — hand off to ParaView with pre-loaded views.

Each step has a green check when it's ready and blocks you from advancing until the previous step is valid. Great for learning the workflow and for building repeatable case templates.

docs.title: 3.6 Compute Engine (HPC clusters)
docs.text:
Icon: CPU · Purpose: connect Eddy to a remote HPC cluster over SSH and run cases there instead of locally.

Once you add an SSH profile (host, user, private key or password, remote workspace path) you can:

  • Upload the current case to the cluster with one click — Eddy rsyncs only what changed.
  • Submit a Slurm or LSF job from a template — Eddy fills in the case path and MPI process count.
  • Watch the remote solver log stream back into the local console, live.
  • Rsync results back to your machine for post-processing when the job finishes.

Tip

For clusters that need MFA or a jump host, put the config in your ~/.ssh/config as you normally would — Eddy reads it and inherits the settings, including ProxyJump chains.

docs.title: 3.7 Cloud Storage
docs.text:
Icon: cloud + gear · Purpose: back up and share cases via cloud providers (S3, Backblaze B2, Google Drive, or your own SFTP/WebDAV).

Useful when you're collaborating with a colleague or moving between machines. Point it at a bucket and drag any case folder into the panel to sync. The panel also handles versioning — you can revert an entire case to how it was three commits ago without leaving Eddy.

Note

Cloud sync is optional. All local functionality (Case Builder, solver runs, ParaView handoff) works fully offline — you only need the internet for the AI copilot and, if you use it, cloud sync.

docs.title: 3.8 AI Extensions
docs.text:
Icon: lightning bolt · Purpose: configure which AI model powers Copilot and, on Free tier, plug in your own API keys.

On the Pro plan this panel is mostly informational — iteraSim provides managed access to Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude Sonnet, routed automatically based on the type of question. You can override the default routing per-request if you want.

On the Free plan you bring your own key from one of:

  • Google Gemini (free 2.5 Flash tier is generous)
  • Anthropic Claude
  • OpenAI GPT
  • Local Ollama for fully-offline use (slower, quality varies by model)

Keys are encrypted at rest with your OS keyring (libsecret on Linux) — not stored in plaintext, not sent to any iteraSim server.

docs.title: 3.9 Copilot panel
docs.text:
Right side of the window · Purpose: the AI chat that reads your case files and can modify them safely.

The Copilot has full read access to whatever case you have open — it sees your controlDict, fvSchemes, boundary files, mesh statistics, and recent solver logs before answering. Ask questions in plain English:

  • "Why is my kOmegaSST diverging after 200 iterations?"
  • "Set up a Boussinesq-buoyant simulation for this geometry."
  • "Fix the boundary conditions so the outlet doesn't back-flow."
  • "Explain what relaxationFactors under 0.3 means for my convergence."

When Copilot suggests a change to a dict file, you get a Preview change button that shows a red/green diff of the exact lines that will be modified. Nothing is written to disk until you approve it. Approved changes are also recorded in a per-case history so you can revert.

Tip

The status bar shows how many tokens you've used this month. Free-tier users see the counter turn amber near 40k tokens and red at 50k. Upgrade to Pro (section 5) for a 100× monthly quota.

docs.title: 3.10 Editor + mesh preview
docs.text:
The centre workspace hosts two things depending on what you're doing:

  • Editor — syntax-highlighted view of any dict/text/STL/log file you open from the Navigator. Auto-saves on blur. Detects when the file changes on disk (e.g. from a solver run) and offers to reload.
  • Preview3D — a lightweight WebGL viewer for meshes and geometry. Rotate with left-drag, pan with right-drag, zoom with the scroll wheel. This is a sanity check, not a post-processing tool — for full contour plots, streamlines, and slicing hand the case to ParaView using the toolbar button.

Note

The Preview3D deliberately doesn't render huge meshes fully — opening a 50-million-cell mesh here would freeze the app. ParaView is the right tool for anything above ~1 million cells.

docs.title: 3.11 Appearance & preferences
docs.text: Bottom-left of the sidebar, palette icon. Change zoom level, text size, theme (dark / light), font family, and the accent colour. All of these persist across sessions and apply immediately — no restart needed.

docs.title: 6 Troubleshooting
docs.text: The most common gotchas, and how to fix them.

docs.title: The app window is blank or black
docs.text:
Usually a GPU driver issue on older Intel or Nvidia cards. Launch Eddy with software rendering:

./iteraSim-Eddy-1.0.0.AppImage --disable-gpu

docs.title: Eddy doesn't appear in my applications menu after first launch
docs.text:
Some desktop environments (older Xfce, i3, sway) don't auto-refresh their app cache. Force a refresh:

update-desktop-database ~/.local/share/applications
gtk-update-icon-cache -t ~/.local/share/icons/hicolor 2>/dev/null || true

Log out and back in if it still doesn't appear. On GNOME and KDE Plasma the menu updates within a few seconds of first launch — no action needed.

docs.title: I moved the AppImage and now the menu icon does nothing
docs.text: The .desktop entry still points at the old location. Launch the AppImage once from its new folder — Eddy detects the move and rewrites the menu entry automatically.

docs.title: "OpenFOAM: not found" in the status bar
docs.text:
Your OpenFOAM install isn't on the login-shell PATH. Two fixes:

  • Install via package manager (see section 1.4).
  • Or edit your ~/.bashrc to source the OpenFOAM etc/bashrc — Eddy detects any version whose bashrc is sourced.

docs.title: Copilot says "No API key configured" — but I'm on Pro
docs.text:
This message is misleading, and it catches Pro users in particular. It is usually not about your API key at all. It means Eddy's local backend is not running.

Look at the status bar at the bottom of the window. If it reads ○ Offline (grey) rather than ● Ready (green), that is the real problem. The LOCAL badge instead of LIVE says the same thing.

Why a Pro subscriber sees it. Your Pro plan's managed model access is served through the local backend — a small Python service Eddy starts for you on 127.0.0.1:8000. When that service isn't running, Eddy falls back to a second path: talking to a model provider directly using a key stored on your machine. If you never set a personal key — and Pro users have no reason to — that fallback has nothing to use, and reports the missing key rather than the missing backend. Your subscription and token balance are untouched; the status bar still shows PRO and your remaining tokens.

The fix, in order:

  1. Click ⟳ Start Backend in the message. Give it five to ten seconds. The status bar should flip to ● Ready and the badge to LIVE. Re-send your question.

  2. If it stays Offline, check whether something else holds port 8000:

    curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/health
ss -ltnp | grep 8000

    A healthy backend answers the first command. If a different program owns the port, close it and press Start Backend again.

  3. Still Offline — restart Eddy completely. The backend is started automatically at launch, so a clean start usually recovers it.

  4. Check AI Extensions (the lightning-bolt icon). The panel has its own ⟳ Restart Backend button and shows the last startup error, which tells you why it failed rather than just that it did.

Common reasons the backend isn't up:

  • First launch after install — Python dependencies are still unpacking. Wait a minute and press Start Backend.
  • Port 8000 already in use — another dev server, or a previous Eddy that didn't exit cleanly.
  • A second Eddy is already running — only one instance can hold the port.
  • Firewall or endpoint security blocking loopback connections. The backend is local-only and never listens on an external interface; allow 127.0.0.1:8000.

Working deliberately offline? Then the message means what it says. Open AI Extensions, add a key for Google Gemini, Anthropic, OpenAI or OpenRouter, or point Eddy at a local Ollama model. That path bypasses the backend entirely and works with no network at all. Keys are stored in your OS keyring, never in plaintext and never on our servers.

Which path am I on?

● Ready / LIVE — the backend is serving requests. Pro users are on managed models and metered tokens. ○ Offline / LOCAL — the backend is down. Eddy uses a personal key if you have one, and the local CFD expert for solver questions if you don't.

Tip

Everything that is not the copilot keeps working while the backend is offline: the Case Builder, blockMesh, snappyHexMesh, Gmsh, running the solver and the ParaView handoff are all local. An Offline badge costs you the AI, not the simulation.

docs.title: Copilot says "monthly token cap reached"
docs.text: You've used all 50,000 free tokens for this calendar month. Either wait for the 1st of next month, or upgrade to Pro (section 5).

docs.title: "Billing is not configured" when clicking Upgrade
docs.text: This means the deployment hasn't wired Stripe yet. If you're the administrator, see BUILD_LINUX.md in the source tree. If you're an end user, email info@iterasim.in — we'll send you a one-off invoice.

docs.title: Solver runs but residuals aren't plotting
docs.text: Eddy needs to see the solver's stdout to plot residuals. If you launched the solver from an external terminal instead of the in-app Run button, the plot panel will stay empty. Use Run in the toolbar.

docs.title: HPC cluster: "Permission denied (publickey)"
docs.text:
Your SSH key isn't on the cluster. Either:

  • Copy your key manually: ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub user@cluster.example.com.
  • Or set the Password field in the SSH profile — Eddy will use it via sshpass.

docs.title: A command fails with "blockMesh: command not found"
docs.text:
The terminal is sourcing an OpenFOAM tree that has not been compiled. This happens when more than one OpenFOAM lives on the machine — typically a source checkout alongside a built install — and the version selector in the title bar is pointing at the wrong one.

The symptom: the command runs in the right directory but the binary is not on PATH. The line above it is the giveaway — No completions for …/platforms/linux64GccDPInt32Opt/bin means that install has no compiled binaries.

Pick the built installation from the OpenFOAM dropdown in the title bar. To see which of your trees is actually built, check for a solver binary:

ls $WM_PROJECT_DIR/platforms/*/bin/blockMesh

docs.title: The case dies instantly with a dictionary error
docs.text:
OpenFOAM is strict about which keywords a solver expects. The three you are most likely to meet, and what each means:

  • Entry 'PISO' not found — the pressure–velocity block does not match the solver family. icoFoam and pisoFoam read a PISO block, pimpleFoam and its relatives a PIMPLE block, and the steady solvers a SIMPLE block.
  • Unable to set reference cell for field p — a fully enclosed domain, where every boundary is a wall, has no pressure datum. Add pRefCell 0; pRefValue 0; to that block.
  • writeInterval < 1 for writeControl timeStep — a steady run counts writes in iterations, so the interval must be a whole number. Fractional intervals belong to transient runs using writeControl runTime.

Note

Cases written by the Case Builder already carry all three settings. You will only hit these when editing dictionaries by hand or importing a case from elsewhere.

docs.title: The solver starts, then diverges
docs.text:
Work through it in this order — it is almost always the first item:

  • Courant number. Keep it below 1, and nearer 0.3 for transient runs. Halve the time step and see whether the blow-up moves.
  • Mesh quality. Run checkMesh; high non-orthogonality or skewness needs matching corrections in fvSchemes.
  • Numerics. Drop the preset to robust (first-order upwind). If that converges, the problem is scheme choice, not the case setup.
  • Boundary conditions. An over-constrained pressure field — for instance a fixed value at both inlet and outlet — will not converge.

docs.title: Copilot replied instantly with a case summary instead of answering
docs.text: A reply that arrives in under a second did not come from the AI. It came from a built-in shortcut, usually a case lookup triggered by a keyword in your message. Rephrase it as a question — start with which, what or how — and ask again. Questions get answered; instructions such as "set up a cavity case" deliberately drive the case pipeline instead.

docs.title: Known limitations in this release
docs.text:
Worth knowing before you plan work around them:

  • Compressible and buoyant cases. rhoSimpleFoam, rhoPimpleFoam, buoyantSimpleFoam and buoyantPimpleFoam appear in the Case Builder but it does not yet write constant/thermophysicalProperties, so those cases need that file added by hand before they will run.
  • Free-form solver generation. Asking Copilot to add an arbitrary equation to any solver is not yet reliable — the generated C++ can reference OpenFOAM API that does not exist. The built-in recipes, such as adding passive temperature transport to simpleFoam, do compile dependably.
  • Copilot advises, it does not compute. Ask it to run an analysis over your files — a mesh-convergence study, say — and you get a method and a script, not computed numbers. Run the script yourself.
  • Knowledge retrieval is offline. Answers come from the language model's own knowledge rather than an indexed OpenFOAM corpus, so verify specific API details against the OpenFOAM source.

docs.title: 5 Upgrading to Pro
docs.text: $29 per month. Cancel any time from the app.

docs.title: 5.1 What Pro unlocks
docs.text:
• 5,000,000 tokens / month (vs 50,000 on Free) — enough for hundreds of long copilot sessions.
  • Curated OpenFOAM knowledge base (RAG) — the copilot cites official OpenFOAM tutorials, foam-extend guides, and vetted forum answers.
  • Managed AI keys — no need to bring your own Gemini or Claude API key. Priority routing between Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude Sonnet.
  • Priority email support at info@iterasim.in.

docs.title: 5.2 How to upgrade
docs.text:
• Click the account icon (top-right) → Pricing. Or type Ctrl+, and pick Plan & billing.
  • Click Upgrade to Pro on the Pro card.
  • Your default web browser opens on Stripe's secure Checkout page. Enter card details there — nothing sensitive is entered into Eddy itself.
  • After paying, close the browser tab and return to Eddy. Your account badge switches to PRO within a few seconds.

Tip

Stripe accepts most cards, Google Pay, and Apple Pay. Corporate cards and VAT numbers are supported — enter them in the Checkout form.

docs.title: 5.3 Managing your subscription
docs.text:
Once you are on Pro, the Pricing dialog shows a Manage subscription button. Clicking it opens Stripe's Customer Portal in your browser, where you can:

  • Update your card.
  • Download past invoices.
  • Cancel — takes effect at the end of the current billing period; you keep Pro until then.
  • Change the email that receives receipts.
